title: Mini Crackme: Find the Passing Input (2026-09-26)
blurb:
Windows x86-64, rcx = pointer to a null-terminated C string. Find a string that makes check return 1:

check:                        ; rcx = string pointer, returns eax (1=pass, 0=fail)
    xor     eax, eax          ; eax = accumulator
    xor     edx, edx          ; edx = index
.loop:
    movzx   r8d, byte [rcx+rdx]
    test    r8d, r8d
    jz      .done
    movzx   r9d, byte [rcx+rdx+1]
    test    r9d, r9d
    jz      .done
    sub     r8d, r9d
    jns     .skip
    neg     r8d
.skip:
    add     eax, r8d
    inc     edx
    jmp     .loop
.done:
    cmp     eax, 0
    sete    al
    ret

--- Answer ---

Any string whose characters are all identical, e.g. "aaaa" (a single character, or even "", also passes).

int check(const char *s) {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; s[i] && s[i+1]; i++)
        sum += abs((int)s[i] - (int)s[i+1]);
    return sum == 0;
}

Explanation: The loop walks adjacent character pairs s[i]/s[i+1], stopping via two null-checks (jz .done) as soon as either byte is the terminator -- a one-char lookahead, not a plain strlen scan. sub/jns/neg is a branching absolute-value idiom (contrast with the branchless sar/xor/sub trick): if the difference is negative, negate it. Since each term added to eax is non-negative, the total can equal zero only if every adjacent pair is equal -- i.e. every character in the string is the same.
